title: week-03
text:
English:
Data visualization helps reveal patterns that summary statistics may hide. Anscombe’s Quartet shows that datasets can have similar means, correlations, and regression lines but still look very different when plotted.
العربي:
الرسوم البيانية تساعدنا نلاحظ أنماط قد لا تظهر من الإحصاءات الملخصة فقط.
العربي:
Anscombe’s Quartet يوضح أن بيانات مختلفة قد يكون عندها متوسط وارتباط وخط انحدار متشابه، لكن شكلها بالرسم مختلف جدًا.




ggplot(data) +
  aes(...) +
  geom_*()
English:
ggplot(data) selects the dataset.
العربي:
ggplot(data) يحدد البيانات التي سنستخدمها.
English:
aes() maps variables to visual properties such as x, y, color, and size.
العربي:
aes() يربط المتغيرات بالمحاور أو اللون أو الحجم.
English:
geom_*() determines how the data are drawn.
العربي:
geom_*() يحدد شكل الرسم.




aes(color = reliability)
English:
Use this when color is connected to a variable.
العربي:
نستخدمه عندما يكون اللون مرتبطًا بمتغير في البيانات.
geom_point(color = "blue")
English:
Use this when all points should have the same fixed color.
العربي:
نستخدمه عندما نريد لونًا ثابتًا لكل النقاط.




geom_histogram()
English:
Shows the distribution of one variable.
العربي:
يعرض توزيع متغير واحد.
geom_point()
English:
Shows the relationship between two variables.
العربي:
يعرض العلاقة بين متغيرين.
geom_boxplot()
English:
Compares groups.
العربي:
يستخدم لمقارنة مجموعات.
geom_col()
English:
Compares values between categories.
العربي:
يستخدم لمقارنة القيم بين الفئات.
geom_line()
English:
Shows change over time.
العربي:
يعرض التغير عبر الزمن.
geom_errorbar()
English:
Shows uncertainty around an estimate.
العربي:
يعرض مقدار عدم اليقين حول التقدير.




[ Estimate MOE ]
English:
The Margin of Error shows uncertainty around an estimate.
العربي:
هامش الخطأ يوضح مقدار عدم اليقين حول التقدير.
Example:
[ 10,000 ]
English:
This gives a range from approximately 9,200 to 10,800.
العربي:
هذا يعطي نطاقًا تقريبيًا من 9,200 إلى 10,800.




moe_pct = moe / estimate * 100
English:
This measures the Margin of Error relative to the estimate.
العربي:
هذا يحسب هامش الخطأ كنسبة من قيمة التقدير.
county_data <- county_data %>%
  mutate(moe_pct = moe / estimate * 100)




county_data <- county_data %>%
  mutate(
    reliability = case_when(
      moe_pct < 5  ~ "High confidence",
      moe_pct < 10 ~ "Moderate",
      TRUE         ~ "Low confidence"
    )
  )
English:
This classifies estimates based on relative uncertainty.
العربي:
هذا يصنف التقديرات حسب مقدار عدم اليقين النسبي.




[ SE = ]
English:
The Standard Error measures sampling uncertainty.
العربي:
الـ Standard Error يقيس عدم اليقين الناتج عن العينة.
med_inc_se = med_incM / 1.645




[ CV = ]
cv = (moe / 1.645) / estimate * 100
English:
CV is a relative measure of sampling error.
العربي:
الـ CV هو مقياس نسبي للخطأ الناتج عن العينة.




case_when(
  cv < 12  ~ "Reliable",
  cv <= 40 ~ "Somewhat reliable",
  TRUE     ~ "Unreliable"
)
English:
Lower CV values indicate higher reliability.
العربي:
كلما انخفضت قيمة CV كانت الموثوقية أعلى.




geom_errorbar(
  aes(
    ymin = estimate - moe,
    ymax = estimate + moe
  )
)
English:
Error bars show the uncertainty around an estimate.
العربي:
أشرطة الخطأ تعرض مقدار عدم اليقين حول التقدير.
English:
A longer error bar means more uncertainty.
العربي:
كلما كان شريط الخطأ أطول كان عدم اليقين أكبر.




sum(estimate)
English:
Use this to add estimates.
العربي:
نستخدمه لجمع التقديرات.
moe_sum(moe, estimate)
English:
Use this to calculate the MOE of a combined estimate.
العربي:
نستخدمه لحساب هامش الخطأ للقيمة المجمعة.
English:
Do not simply add MOEs together.
العربي:
لا نجمع قيم MOE جمعًا مباشرًا.




moe_prop()
English:
Use moe_prop() when the numerator is part of the denominator.
العربي:
نستخدم moe_prop() عندما يكون البسط جزءًا من المقام.
Example:
People below poverty / Total population




moe_ratio()
English:
Use moe_ratio() when dividing two different quantities.
العربي:
نستخدم moe_ratio() عندما نقسم كميتين مختلفتين.
Example:
Population / Households
English:
The numerator is not a subset of the denominator.
العربي:
هنا البسط ليس جزءًا من المقام.




English:
When comparing ACS 5-year estimates, use non-overlapping periods.
العربي:
عند مقارنة تقديرات ACS لخمس سنوات يفضل استخدام فترات غير متداخلة.
Better comparison:
2014–2018 vs 2019–2023
Less appropriate comparison:
2018–2022 vs 2019–2023
English:
The second comparison contains several overlapping years.
العربي:
المقارنة الثانية تحتوي على سنوات مشتركة كثيرة.




change = new_estimate - old_estimate
English:
A positive value means an increase.
العربي:
القيمة الموجبة تعني زيادة.
English:
A negative value means a decrease.
العربي:
القيمة السالبة تعني انخفاض.




se_1 = moe_1 / 1.645
se_2 = moe_2 / 1.645
se_diff = sqrt(se_1^2 + se_2^2)
English:
This combines uncertainty from both periods.
العربي:
هذا يجمع مقدار عدم اليقين من الفترتين.




z = change / se_diff
significant = abs(z) > 1.645
English:
We use the absolute value of the z-score.
العربي:
نستخدم القيمة المطلقة للـ z-score.
English:
If abs(z) > 1.645, the change is statistically significant.
العربي:
إذا كانت القيمة المطلقة للـ z أكبر من 1.645، فالتغير يعتبر ذا دلالة إحصائية.




moe_diff = se_diff * 1.645
[ Change MOE_{diff} ]
English:
If the confidence interval includes zero, the change is not statistically significant.
العربي:
إذا كانت فترة الثقة تحتوي على الصفر، فالتغير غير دال إحصائيًا.
English:
If the interval does not include zero, the change is statistically significant.
العربي:
إذا كانت فترة الثقة لا تحتوي على الصفر، فالتغير دال إحصائيًا.




bind_rows(
  get_poverty(2018),
  get_poverty(2023)
)
English:
bind_rows() stacks datasets vertically.
العربي:
bind_rows() يجمع الجداول فوق بعض بالصفوف.




pivot_wider(
  names_from = period,
  values_from = c(estimate, moe)
)
English:
pivot_wider() converts data from long format to wide format.
العربي:
pivot_wider() يحول البيانات من الشكل الطولي إلى الشكل العريض.
English:
This makes it easier to compare years side by side.
العربي:
هذا يجعل مقارنة السنوات جنبًا إلى جنب أسهل.




arrange(desc(moe_pct))
English:
Sorts rows based on a variable.
العربي:
يرتب الصفوف حسب متغير معين.
English:
desc() sorts from largest to smallest.
العربي:
desc() يرتب من الأكبر إلى الأصغر.




slice_head(n = 15)
English:
Keeps the first 15 rows.
العربي:
يأخذ أول 15 صفًا.




reorder(NAME, estimate)
English:
Reorders categories based on the value of another variable.
العربي:
يعيد ترتيب الفئات حسب قيمة متغير آخر.




coord_flip()
English:
Flips the x and y axes.
العربي:
يقلب المحورين x و y.
English:
This is useful when category names are long.
العربي:
هذا مفيد عندما تكون أسماء الفئات طويلة.




mutate(
  NAME = str_remove(NAME, " County, New York")
)
English:
Removes repeated text from names.
العربي:
يحذف النص المتكرر من أسماء المناطق.




theme_minimal()
English:
Uses a cleaner and simpler chart theme.
العربي:
يستخدم شكلًا أبسط وأنظف للرسم.




geometry = TRUE
English:
Adding geometry = TRUE returns ACS data with spatial geometry.
العربي:
إضافة geometry = TRUE تجعل بيانات ACS تحتوي على المعلومات المكانية.
Example:
philly_tracts <- get_acs(
  geography = "tract",
  state = "PA",
  county = "Philadelphia",
  variables = c(
    med_inc = "B19013_001",
    total_pop = "B01003_001"
  ),
  year = 2023,
  output = "wide",
  geometry = TRUE
)




class(philly_tracts)
English:
The data can now behave as an sf spatial object.
العربي:
البيانات الآن يمكن التعامل معها ككائن مكاني من نوع sf.
English:
The geometry column contains the spatial shapes.
العربي:
عمود geometry يحتوي على الأشكال المكانية للمناطق.




ggplot(philly_tracts) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = ...))
English:
geom_sf() is used to draw spatial features such as census tracts.
العربي:
geom_sf() يستخدم لرسم العناصر المكانية مثل Census Tracts.
English:
The fill aesthetic can represent a variable across different geographic areas.
العربي:
يمكن استخدام fill لتمثيل متغير مختلف من منطقة جغرافية إلى أخرى.




English:
This week connected statistical reliability with spatial analysis. ACS estimates should not be treated as exact numbers without considering uncertainty.
العربي:
هذا الأسبوع ربط بين الموثوقية الإحصائية والتحليل المكاني.
العربي:
تقديرات ACS لا يجب التعامل معها كأرقام دقيقة تمامًا بدون النظر إلى مقدار عدم اليقين.
English:
MOE, SE, and CV help evaluate reliability before interpreting or mapping estimates.
العربي:
تساعد MOE وSE وCV في تقييم موثوقية البيانات قبل تفسيرها أو عرضها على الخريطة.
English:
Adding geometry allows statistical ACS data to become spatial data that can be mapped using geom_sf().
العربي:
إضافة Geometry تسمح بتحويل بيانات ACS الإحصائية إلى بيانات مكانية يمكن رسمها باستخدام geom_sf().

The live website: What visitors see through GitHub Pages.



Repository
Pronunciation: ri-POZ-uh-tor-ee

Markdown and R Symbols

* is called an asterisk. In Markdown, it adds emphasis such as italics or bold. In R, it represents multiplication.

Philadelphia’s tract-level poverty data show that changes over time are uneven and often uncertain. Between the 2006–2010 and 2013–2017 ACS 5-year periods, only 63 of 376 testable census tracts showed a statistically significant change in poverty rate.
Because the article does not identify which census tracts were combined to define Eastwick, its specific neighborhood-level claim cannot be directly verified with the available tract-level data. title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:
The question
Every number the American Community Survey publishes is an estimate drawn from a sample, not a count. That means every number comes with a margin of error — a statement about how wrong it might be.
Most people ignore it. In this assignment, you won’t.
In this analysis, I examine median home values across counties in Texas and ask which counties are measured most and least reliably. I chose this topic because my experience in major infrastructure and urban development projects has increased my interest in understanding how development outcomes differ across communities.

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:
What this means for policy
The results show that some small counties in Texas have less reliable estimates of median home values than larger counties. Presidio County has the highest relative margin of error at 63.9%. It is followed by Motley County at 59.5% and Kent County at 56.5%. Crockett, Childress, and Sterling counties also have high margins of error. This means we should be careful when using the estimates for these counties because the real values may be different from the published estimates.
This pattern is connected to the way the American Community Survey works. The ACS does not count every person or home. Instead, it uses a sample to estimate values for the whole community. Smaller counties usually have fewer people and homes in the sample, so their estimates have more uncertainty. In my results, high-confidence counties have an average population of 482,559, while low-confidence counties have an average population of only 6,426. Moderate-confidence counties have an average population of 28,971. This shows a clear relationship between smaller population and lower reliability.
This uncertainty can cause problems if a state agency uses median home value to distribute funding and assumes every county estimate is equally accurate. If a small county’s home value is overestimated, it may appear wealthier and receive less funding than it needs. Rural and small communities may therefore be affected the most. Agencies should consider both the estimate and its margin of error before making funding decisions.

Where Code Lives

Console: Useful for testing commands, but the code is not saved.
R script: Stores code in a reusable file.
Code chunk: Places executable code inside a Quarto document.
Comment: Text after # explains the code and is not executed.

title: Week 2: dplyr and Census Data

Objects, Functions, and Arguments
result <- filter(counties, population > 50000) # Keep larger counties

result is the object that stores the output.
<- is the assignment arrow.
filter() is the function or verb.
counties is the input data.
population > 50000 is the condition or argument.
# begins a comment that R does not execute.

title: Week 2: dplyr and Census Data
text:
Packages
A package adds tools and functions to R.
install.packages("dplyr")
Installation is normally completed once.
library(dplyr)
library(tidycensus)
The required package must be loaded again when starting a new R session.

title: Week 2: dplyr and Census Data
text:
Data Frames and Tibbles
A data frame organizes information into rows and columns.

Row: An observation, such as one county.
Column: A variable, such as population, income, or margin of error.
Tibble: A modern data frame that prints results more clearly.

Most dplyr verbs take a tibble as input and return another tibble as output.

Purpose

title: Week 2: dplyr and Census Data
text:
Pipes
The pipe %>% sends the result of one step into the next step.
new_data <- counties %>%
  filter(moe_pct > 10) %>%
  arrange(desc(moe_pct)) %>%
  select(NAME, moe_pct)
This code keeps counties with a margin of error above 10 percent, sorts them from highest to lowest, and displays only the county name and margin-of-error percentage.

title: Week 2: dplyr and Census Data
text:
Census and ACS Data
The Decennial Census happens every ten years and aims to count the full population using a short questionnaire.
The American Community Survey is conducted continuously and uses a sample to produce estimates about population, housing, income, education, and other community characteristics.

ACS 1-year estimates: More current and available for places with populations of 65,000 or more.
ACS 3-year estimates: Discontinued.
ACS 5-year estimates: Combine five years of responses and are available for smaller geographic areas.
Every ACS estimate should be considered together with its margin of error.

title: Week 2: dplyr and Census Data
text:
Geographic Levels
Census geography moves from larger to smaller areas:
State → County → Census Tract → Block Group → Block
Smaller geographic areas usually contain smaller samples and may have larger margins of error. Geographic boundaries can also change over time, which can make comparisons between years more difficult.

title: Week 2: dplyr and Census Data
text:
Getting ACS Data
The tidycensus package connects R to Census data.
data <- get_acs(
  geography = "county",
  variables = "B19013_001",
  state = "TX",
  year = 2023,
  survey = "acs5"
)
The load_variables() function can be used to search for available ACS variables.

title: Week 2: dplyr and Census Data
text:
Understanding Variable Codes
For the code B19013_001:

B identifies a detailed base table.
19013 identifies the table.
001 identifies the line within the table.
E means estimate when it appears in a wide result.
M means margin of error when it appears in a wide result.

title: Week 2: dplyr and Census Data
text:
Long and Wide Data
In long format, each variable appears in a separate row with columns such as:

GEOID
NAME
variable
estimate
moe

In wide format, multiple variables appear in the same row. Column names may include E for estimate and M for margin of error.

ملاحظاتي


كتابة الأوامر وحفظها

نافذة الأوامر مناسبة لتجربة التعليمات بسرعة، لكن ما أكتبه فيها لا يُحفظ تلقائيًا.
ملف الأوامر يحفظ الكود حتى أستطيع الرجوع إليه وتشغيله مرة أخرى.
يمكن وضع الكود داخل مستند يحتوي أيضًا على الشرح والنتائج.
النص المكتوب بعد علامة التعليق يشرح الكود ولا يتم تشغيله.



مكونات الأمر

الكائن هو الاسم الذي نستخدمه لحفظ البيانات أو النتيجة.
سهم الإسناد ينقل النتيجة ويحفظها داخل الكائن.
الدالة هي العملية التي نريد تنفيذها على البيانات.
المدخلات هي البيانات التي ستُطبق عليها العملية.
الوسيط يحدد الشرط أو الخيار المستخدم داخل الدالة.



الحزم البرمجية

الحزمة البرمجية تضيف أدوات ودوال جديدة إلى البرنامج.
يتم تثبيت الحزمة عادة مرة واحدة على الجهاز.
يجب تحميل الحزمة عند بدء جلسة جديدة قبل استخدام دوالها.
إذا ظهرت رسالة بأن الدالة غير موجودة، فقد يكون السبب أن الحزمة لم تُحمّل.



تنظيم البيانات

يتكون جدول البيانات من صفوف وأعمدة.
يمثل كل صف مشاهدة واحدة، مثل مقاطعة واحدة.
يمثل كل عمود متغيرًا، مثل عدد السكان أو قيمة المنزل أو هامش الخطأ.
يمكن اختيار الصفوف التي تحقق شرطًا محددًا.
يمكن اختيار الأعمدة المطلوبة فقط.
يمكن إنشاء عمود جديد من خلال عملية حسابية.
يمكن ترتيب النتائج من الأصغر إلى الأكبر أو من الأكبر إلى الأصغر.
يمكن تقسيم البيانات إلى مجموعات ثم حساب ملخص لكل مجموعة.



تسلسل خطوات التحليل

يمكن ربط عدة عمليات بحيث تنتقل نتيجة الخطوة الأولى إلى الخطوة التالية.
يساعد هذا الأسلوب على قراءة التحليل بالترتيب بدل إنشاء نتيجة منفصلة لكل خطوة.
في الواجب قمنا بحساب نسبة هامش الخطأ، ثم ترتيب المقاطعات، ثم تصنيفها حسب الموثوقية.



بيانات السكان

يتم إجراء التعداد السكاني الشامل كل عشر سنوات بهدف عد السكان.
مسح المجتمع الأمريكي يُجرى بصورة مستمرة ويعتمد على عينة من المجتمع.
يوفر المسح معلومات عن السكان والسكن والدخل والتعليم وخصائص أخرى.
البيانات المنشورة من المسح هي تقديرات وليست أعدادًا مؤكدة بالكامل.
يأتي كل تقدير مع هامش خطأ يوضح مقدار عدم اليقين فيه.
تشمل تقديرات السنوات الخمس المجتمعات والمناطق الجغرافية الصغيرة.
لا تعني تقديرات السنوات الخمس أنها بيانات سنة واحدة، بل تجمع استجابات خلال خمس سنوات.



المستويات الجغرافية

تبدأ المستويات الجغرافية بالولاية ثم المقاطعة ثم المناطق الإحصائية الأصغر.
كلما صغر المستوى الجغرافي، صغر حجم العينة غالبًا وارتفع هامش الخطأ.
قد تتغير الحدود الجغرافية مع مرور الوقت، ولذلك يجب الحذر عند المقارنة بين سنوات مختلفة.



التقدير وهامش الخطأ

التقدير هو القيمة التي ينتجها المسح بناءً على العينة.
هامش الخطأ يوضح مقدار احتمال اختلاف القيمة الحقيقية عن التقدير.
لا تكفي مقارنة هامش الخطأ كرقم فقط، لأن حجم التقدير يختلف بين المقاطعات.
يمكن قسمة هامش الخطأ على التقدير وضرب الناتج في مئة للحصول على نسبة مئوية.
كلما ارتفعت هذه النسبة، انخفضت موثوقية التقدير.
المقاطعات الصغيرة قد تظهر فيها نسب خطأ أعلى بسبب قلة عدد المشاهدات في العينة.



ما تعلمته من التطبيق

تعلمت أن الحصول على البيانات ليس نهاية التحليل؛ يجب تقييم دقتها قبل استخدامها.
أظهرت النتائج أن المقاطعات ذات عدد السكان الأقل كانت أقل موثوقية في المتوسط.
لا ينبغي معاملة جميع المقاطعات كأن بياناتها متساوية في الدقة.
قد يؤدي تجاهل عدم اليقين إلى توزيع غير عادل للتمويل أو اتخاذ قرار غير مناسب.
يرتبط هذا بخبرتي في الجودة وإدارة المخاطر، لأن القرار الجيد يعتمد على بيانات موثوقة.
يمكن التعامل مع هامش الخطأ كمؤشر للمخاطر يساعد على تحديد النتائج التي تحتاج إلى حذر أكبر.
Code

1. Spatial Data and sf
Spatial data is data that includes information about location.
البيانات المكانية هي بيانات تحتوي على معلومات عن الموقع.
In R, spatial data is commonly handled using the sf package.
في R يتم التعامل مع البيانات المكانية عادة باستخدام حزمة sf.
An sf object is basically a normal data frame with an additional geometry column.
كائن sf هو بشكل أساسي جدول بيانات عادي يحتوي على عمود إضافي يسمى geometry.
The geometry column stores the spatial shape of each observation.
عمود geometry يخزن الشكل المكاني لكل مشاهدة.
Geometry can represent points, lines, or polygons.
الهندسة المكانية يمكن أن تمثل نقاطا أو خطوطا أو مضلعات.
The geometry column usually stays attached to the data even when other columns are selected.
عمود geometry عادة يبقى مرتبطا بالبيانات حتى عند اختيار أعمدة أخرى.
If geometry is no longer needed, it can be removed using st_drop_geometry.
إذا لم نعد بحاجة إلى الهندسة المكانية يمكن إزالتها باستخدام st_drop_geometry.

2. Coordinate Reference Systems
A Coordinate Reference System tells R how spatial coordinates should be interpreted.
نظام الإسناد الإحداثي يحدد لـ R كيفية تفسير الإحداثيات المكانية.
The abbreviation is CRS.
الاختصار هو CRS.
There are two main types of coordinate systems.
يوجد نوعان رئيسيان من أنظمة الإحداثيات.
A geographic coordinate system uses longitude and latitude.
نظام الإحداثيات الجغرافي يستخدم خطوط الطول والعرض.
Its units are usually degrees.
وحداته تكون عادة بالدرجات.
A projected coordinate system represents the Earth on a flat surface using X and Y coordinates.
نظام الإحداثيات المسقط يمثل الأرض على سطح مستو باستخدام إحداثيات X و Y.
Its units can be feet or meters.
وحداته يمكن أن تكون بالقدم أو بالمتر.
Projected systems are generally better for measuring distance and area.
الأنظمة المسقطة تكون أفضل عادة لحساب المسافات والمساحات.

3. Projections and Distortion
The Earth is curved, but maps are flat.
الأرض منحنية ولكن الخرائط مسطحة.
Because of this, every map projection creates some type of distortion.
لهذا السبب كل إسقاط خرائطي ينتج نوعا من التشوه.
A projection may focus on preserving shape, area, distance, or direction.
قد يركز الإسقاط على الحفاظ على الشكل أو المساحة أو المسافة أو الاتجاه.
A conformal projection focuses on shape.
الإسقاط المتوافق يركز على الحفاظ على الشكل.
An equal-area projection focuses on area.
الإسقاط متساوي المساحة يركز على الحفاظ على المساحة.
An equidistant projection focuses on certain distances.
الإسقاط متساوي المسافة يركز على الحفاظ على بعض المسافات.
Common projection concepts include cylindrical, conic, and transverse cylindrical projections.
من أشكال الإسقاط الشائعة الإسقاط الأسطواني والمخروطي والأسطواني المستعرض.

4. CRS Rules for Spatial Analysis
The most important rule is that spatial layers should use the same CRS before spatial analysis.
أهم قاعدة هي أن الطبقات المكانية يجب أن تستخدم نفس نظام الإحداثيات قبل التحليل المكاني.
The general workflow is:
الترتيب العام هو:
Check the CRS.
تحقق من نظام الإحداثيات.
Transform the CRS if necessary.
حول نظام الإحداثيات إذا كان ذلك ضروريا.
Then perform measurements.
بعد ذلك قم بالقياسات.
A map can look correct even when the CRS is inappropriate for measurement.
قد تبدو الخريطة صحيحة حتى عندما يكون نظام الإحداثيات غير مناسب للقياس.
Matching CRS values are also not enough if the units are degrees.
تطابق نظام الإحداثيات لا يكفي إذا كانت الوحدات بالدرجات.
Distances, buffers, and areas should normally be calculated using a projected CRS.
المسافات والمناطق العازلة والمساحات يجب عادة حسابها باستخدام نظام إحداثيات مسقط.

5. Philadelphia CRS
For local work in Philadelphia, the class uses Pennsylvania South State Plane.
للعمل المحلي في فيلادلفيا يستخدم الكلاس نظام Pennsylvania South State Plane.
EPSG 2272 uses US feet.
EPSG 2272 يستخدم القدم الأمريكية.
Another version of the same general State Plane zone uses meters.
يوجد إصدار آخر من نفس منطقة State Plane يستخدم المتر.
The unit matters because a distance value has a different meaning in feet and meters.
وحدة القياس مهمة لأن قيمة المسافة تختلف إذا كانت بالقدم أو بالمتر.
Always check the units before calculating distance, area, or buffers.
تحقق دائما من الوحدة قبل حساب المسافات أو المساحات أو المناطق العازلة.

6. Joining Data
There are two important ways to connect data.
يوجد طريقتان مهمتان لربط البيانات.
The first is joining by an identifier.
الطريقة الأولى هي الربط باستخدام معرف.
For Census data, GEOID is commonly used.
في بيانات التعداد يتم استخدام GEOID بشكل شائع.
A left join keeps all rows from the first table and adds matching information from the second table.
الربط من النوع left join يحتفظ بجميع صفوف الجدول الأول ويضيف البيانات المطابقة من الجدول الثاني.
If no match exists, the result can contain NA.
إذا لم يوجد تطابق فقد تظهر القيمة NA.
The second method is joining by location.
الطريقة الثانية هي الربط حسب الموقع.
A spatial join can determine which tract contains a station or another spatial feature.
الربط المكاني يمكن أن يحدد منطقة التعداد التي تحتوي على محطة أو عنصر مكاني آخر.
In spatial analysis, both joining by ID and joining by location are useful.
في التحليل المكاني نحتاج إلى الربط حسب المعرف والربط حسب الموقع.

7. Spatial Relationships
Spatial functions can test how geometries relate to each other.
الدوال المكانية يمكن أن تختبر العلاقة بين الأشكال.
st_intersects checks whether two geometries intersect in any way.
st_intersects تتحقق مما إذا كان هناك أي تقاطع بين شكلين.
st_touches checks whether geometries touch at their boundaries.
st_touches تتحقق مما إذا كانت الأشكال تتلامس عند الحدود.
st_within checks whether one geometry is completely inside another.
st_within تتحقق مما إذا كان شكل موجودا بالكامل داخل شكل آخر.
These tests usually produce logical results such as TRUE or FALSE.
هذه الاختبارات تنتج عادة نتائج منطقية مثل TRUE أو FALSE.
A spatial feature also intersects itself.
العنصر المكاني يتقاطع أيضا مع نفسه.

8. Filter, Intersection, and Union
st_filter selects whole spatial features.
st_filter تختار العناصر المكانية كاملة.
The geometry itself is not cut.
الشكل نفسه لا يتم قصه.
st_intersection creates the actual overlapping area between geometries.
st_intersection تنشئ منطقة التداخل الفعلية بين الأشكال.
This can change the shape of the original geometry.
هذا يمكن أن يغير شكل الهندسة الأصلية.
st_union combines multiple geometries into one geometry.
st_union تدمج عدة أشكال مكانية في شكل واحد.
A useful example is combining many station service areas into one larger service zone.
من الأمثلة المفيدة دمج مناطق الخدمة حول عدة محطات في منطقة خدمة واحدة.

9. Buffers and Transit Access
A buffer creates an area around a spatial feature.
المنطقة العازلة تنشئ مساحة حول عنصر مكاني.
A buffer can be used to represent a service area around a transit station.
يمكن استخدام المنطقة العازلة لتمثيل منطقة خدمة حول محطة نقل.
In US feet, half a mile equals 2640 feet.
عند استخدام القدم الأمريكية فإن نصف ميل يساوي 2640 قدما.
The CRS units must be checked before using this distance.
يجب التأكد من وحدة نظام الإحداثيات قبل استخدام هذه المسافة.
Transit access can be defined in different ways.
يمكن تعريف الوصول إلى النقل بعدة طرق.
One definition is whether the tract centroid is within a certain distance of a station.
أحد التعريفات هو أن يكون مركز منطقة التعداد ضمن مسافة معينة من المحطة.
Another definition is whether the tract touches the service zone.
تعريف آخر هو أن تلامس منطقة التعداد منطقة الخدمة.
Another definition is the percentage of the tract area covered by the service zone.
تعريف آخر هو نسبة مساحة منطقة التعداد الموجودة داخل منطقة الخدمة.
Different definitions can produce different results.
التعريفات المختلفة يمكن أن تنتج نتائج مختلفة.
Choosing a spatial definition is therefore part of the analytical and policy decision.
اختيار التعريف المكاني يعتبر جزءا من القرار التحليلي والسياساتي.

10. Distance and Nearest Features
st_distance calculates spatial distance.
st_distance تحسب المسافة المكانية.
When many features exist in both layers, the result can be a distance matrix.
عندما توجد عدة عناصر في كل طبقة قد تكون النتيجة مصفوفة مسافات.
A distance matrix compares every feature in one layer with every feature in the other layer.
مصفوفة المسافات تقارن كل عنصر في طبقة مع كل عنصر في الطبقة الأخرى.
Sometimes we only need the nearest feature.
في بعض الأحيان نحتاج فقط إلى أقرب عنصر.
st_nearest_feature identifies the nearest spatial feature.
st_nearest_feature تحدد أقرب عنصر مكاني.
A tract centroid can be used as a representative center point when measuring distance to a station.
يمكن استخدام مركز منطقة التعداد كنقطة تمثل المنطقة عند حساب المسافة إلى المحطة.
In EPSG 2272, distances are measured in US feet.
في EPSG 2272 يتم قياس المسافات بالقدم الأمريكية.
There are 5280 feet in one mile.
يوجد 5280 قدما في الميل الواحد.

11. Areas and Coverage
st_area calculates the area of a spatial feature.
st_area تحسب مساحة العنصر المكاني.
With EPSG 2272, areas are measured in square feet.
عند استخدام EPSG 2272 يتم قياس المساحات بالقدم المربع.
One acre equals 43,560 square feet.
الفدان الواحد يساوي 43,560 قدما مربعا.
One square mile equals 27,878,400 square feet.
الميل المربع الواحد يساوي 27,878,400 قدما مربعا.
Area can also be used to calculate how much of a tract is covered by a service zone.
يمكن استخدام المساحة لحساب نسبة منطقة التعداد التي تغطيها منطقة الخدمة.
When two areas use the same unit, the units cancel when calculating a percentage.
عندما تستخدم المساحتان نفس الوحدة فإن الوحدات تلغى عند حساب النسبة.

12. Mapping Spatial Data
Spatial data can be mapped using geometry.
يمكن رسم البيانات المكانية باستخدام الهندسة المكانية.
A good map should focus attention on the important information.
الخريطة الجيدة يجب أن توجه الانتباه إلى المعلومات المهمة.
Unnecessary grid lines, axes, and heavy polygon borders can make a map harder to read.
خطوط الشبكة والمحاور وحدود المضلعات السميكة قد تجعل الخريطة أصعب في القراءة.
Missing values should be shown clearly instead of silently disappearing.
يجب إظهار القيم المفقودة بوضوح بدلا من اختفائها بدون تفسير.
Continuous colors are useful for showing gradual change.
الألوان المستمرة مفيدة لعرض التغير التدريجي.
Classed maps divide values into a small number of groups.
الخرائط المصنفة تقسم القيم إلى عدد صغير من الفئات.
Around four to six meaningful classes are usually easier to interpret.
استخدام أربع إلى ست فئات ذات معنى يكون عادة أسهل في التفسير.
For choropleth maps, rates are usually more meaningful than raw counts.
في الخرائط التدرجية تكون النسب عادة أكثر معنى من الأعداد الخام.

13. Main Week 4 Takeaways
An sf object is still a data frame, but it also contains geometry.
كائن sf لا يزال جدول بيانات ولكنه يحتوي أيضا على هندسة مكانية.
CRS tells us how the coordinates should be interpreted.
CRS يحدد كيفية تفسير الإحداثيات.
Use the same CRS before comparing spatial layers.
استخدم نفس نظام الإحداثيات قبل مقارنة الطبقات المكانية.
Use projected units before measuring distance or area.
استخدم نظام إحداثيات مسقط قبل حساب المسافات أو المساحات.
Know the difference between joining by ID and joining by location.
اعرف الفرق بين الربط باستخدام المعرف والربط باستخدام الموقع.
Know the difference between selecting whole features and cutting overlapping geometry.
اعرف الفرق بين اختيار الأشكال كاملة وقص منطقة التداخل.
Spatial definitions can change the answer to a policy question.
التعريفات المكانية يمكن أن تغير الإجابة عن سؤال سياساتي.

text:
This is not a competition. There’s no leaderboard and no target RMSE. The goal is to practice the full prediction workflow on a question you choose, and to find out what actually helps. Some features you’re sure will help won’t, and some you add on a whim will. Both are findings.
You’ll:

Choose a tract-level outcome for Philadelphia and check whether it’s reliable enough to model (Weeks 2–3).
Fit a baseline model and cross-validate it (Week 5).
Pull data from Philadelphia’s open data portal through its API and build spatial features: counts, densities, and distances (Week 4, plus one new tool).
Transform variables with logs, squared terms, and categories. Watch the October 9 recorded lecture before Part 5.
Keep a model log the whole way through, and compare where your first and final models go wrong.

Timing. Parts 1–4 use only what we’ve covered through Week 5. You can finish them before the October 9 lecture. Part 5 is new material; the lecture explains it, and the instructions below give you the essentials.
Type the code yourself. The worked examples show the pattern. Your job is to apply it to your outcome and your data choices.








Important1. Don’t drop rows



Every model is cross-validated on the same tracts with the same folds, so the rows in your model log are comparable. If a new variable has missing values, fill them (for example, 0 for a count, or the median with a note) or choose a different variable. The cv_rmse() helper below will stop and tell you if you break this rule.


Your outcome comes from the 2019–2023 ACS. Pull open data from 2023 or earlier (2021–2023 is ideal). Using 2025 data to predict a 2023 outcome uses information from the future, which a real prediction model would never have.



Don’t use any variable that’s built from your outcome or measures the same thing another way. Ask yourself: would an agency trying to predict this outcome for a tract have this variable? If the answer is “only because it’s basically the outcome,” leave it out.

text:
Part 0: Setup


Code
library(tidyverse)
library(tidycensus)
library(sf)
library(caret)

Sys.getenv("CENSUS_API_KEY") != ""   # should print TRUE


[1] TRUE



The cross-validation helper
This function runs 10-fold cross-validation with the same seed every time, so every model in your log is tested on the same folds. You don’t need to change it. Read it once so you know what it does.


Code
ctrl <- trainControl(method = "cv", number = 10)

cv_rmse <- function(formula, data) {
  df <- if (inherits(data, "sf")) st_drop_geometry(data) else data
  vars <- all.vars(formula)
  bad <- vars[sapply(vars, function(v) any(is.na(df[[v]])))]
  if (length(bad) > 0) {
    stop("These variables have NAs: ", paste(bad, collapse = ", "),
         ". Fill them or choose another variable (Rule 1: don't drop rows).")
  }
  set.seed(5080)
  fit <- train(formula, data = df, method = "lm", trControl = ctrl)
  fit$results$RMSE
}




The model log
Every time you fit a new model, add a row. By the end, this table is the story of your assignment.


Code
model_log <- tibble(
  model   = character(),
  added   = character(),
  cv_rmse = numeric(),
  notes   = character()
)

The baseline residual map shows that prediction errors are not evenly distributed across Philadelphia. These patterns suggest that socioeconomic characteristics alone may not capture important geographic differences in commuting conditions. Factors such as transit accessibility, proximity to employment centers, and the spatial distribution of transportation infrastructure may help explain some of the remaining errors.

section: Part 3: Getting data from Philadelphia’s open data portal
text:
Part 3: Getting data from Philadelphia’s open data portal
Many of the city’s datasets on OpenDataPhilly are served through a Carto SQL API. You send a SQL query in a URL, and it sends back data. Ask for format=GeoJSON and st_read() reads the result directly, just like the Indego feed in Week 4.
The pattern:
https://phl.carto.com/api/v2/sql?format=GeoJSON&q=SELECT ... FROM table_name WHERE ...
Three pieces of SQL are all you need:

SELECT the_geom, column1, column2 chooses which columns come back. Always include the_geom, or you get no geometry.
FROM table_name chooses the dataset.
WHERE ... filters rows. Filter in the query, not in R. Some tables have millions of rows, and pulling everything will be slow or fail.

This helper builds the URL for you. Spaces and symbols in a URL need encoding, and URLencode() handles that.


Code
carto_get <- function(sql) {
  url <- paste0("https://phl.carto.com/api/v2/sql?format=GeoJSON&q=", URLencode(sql))
  st_read(url, quiet = TRUE)
}



Finding a table name
On a dataset’s OpenDataPhilly page, look for the API link. The table name is the word after FROM in the example query. To see what values a column takes before you filter on it, ask for a count in CSV format:


Code
# What kinds of crime are in the incidents table in 2023?

              URLencode("SELECT text_general_code, COUNT(*) AS n

Why These Spatial Layers?
Two spatial datasets from 2023 were selected to investigate geographic factors that may help explain differences in mean commute time across Philadelphia.
The first dataset contains 13,662 geocoded street defect reports. These reports provide a potential indicator of roadway maintenance conditions that may affect travel experiences but are not directly represented by the ACS socioeconomic predictors.
The second dataset contains 3,681 geocoded residential burglary incidents. Their spatial distribution may capture aspects of neighborhood conditions that are not fully reflected in income, educational attainment, renter occupancy, or vehicle availability.
These variables are exploratory indicators rather than direct measures of commute time or causal effects. The next step is to evaluate whether features derived from these locations improve cross-validated prediction accuracy.

text:
Part 4: Building spatial features
Every feature below reuses a Week 4 tool. The worked examples use burglaries and Indego stations; you build the same types from your own layers.

4A: Counting
How many burglaries fall in each tract?


Code
# Count residential burglaries in each census tract
tracts <- tracts %>%
  mutate(
    n_burglary = lengths(st_intersects(geometry, layer1))
  )

# Summarize burglary counts across tracts
summary(tracts$n_burglary)


   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
  0.000   4.000   7.000   9.458  13.000  48.000 


A tract with no burglaries gets 0, not NA, so Rule 1 is safe.


4B: Density: don’t skip this
Raw counts mostly measure tract size. A big tract has more of everything. Normalize by area, by population, or by housing units, depending on what makes sense for the thing you’re counting.


Code
tracts <- tracts %>%
  mutate(
    area_sqmi = as.numeric(st_area(geometry)) / 27878400,

    burglary_per_sqmi = if_else(
      area_sqmi > 0,
      n_burglary / area_sqmi,
      NA_real_
    ),

    burglary_per_1k = if_else(
      total_popE > 0,
      n_burglary / total_popE * 1000,
      NA_real_
    )
  )

summary(tracts$burglary_per_sqmi)


   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
   0.00   13.70   33.70   53.07   70.32  367.98 


Code
summary(tracts$burglary_per_1k)


   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
  0.000   1.021   1.857   2.528   3.234  16.370 








NotePer capita in low-population tracts



If a tract has 40 residents and 3 burglaries, its rate is 75 per 1,000, which is a huge number built on tiny counts. Look at the tracts with the highest per-capita rates before you trust them. This is the Week 3 lesson about small denominators again.




4C: Measuring distance to the nearest thing
How far is each tract from its nearest Indego station? Use the Week 4 pattern: find the nearest feature, then measure to it element by element.


Code
# Create a point inside each census tract
tract_pts <- st_point_on_surface(tracts)

# Find the nearest street defect report from 2023
nearest_idx <- st_nearest_feature(tract_pts, layer2)

# Calculate distance in miles
tracts <- tracts %>%
  mutate(
    dist_defect_mi = as.numeric(
      st_distance(
        tract_pts,
        layer2[nearest_idx, ],
        by_element = TRUE
      )
    ) / 5280
  )

# Review distance distribution
summary(tracts$dist_defect_mi)


    Min.  1st Qu.   Median     Mean  3rd Qu.     Max. 
0.001716 0.034653 0.060649 0.077200 0.096347 0.567242 




4D: Measuring distance to one place
Sometimes the “thing” is a single location, such as City Hall as a stand-in for the center of the regional economy.


Code
# Philadelphia City Hall coordinates
city_hall <- st_sfc(
  st_point(c(-75.1636, 39.9526)),
  crs = 4326
) %>%
  st_transform(st_crs(tracts))

# Calculate distance to City Hall in miles
tracts <- tracts %>%
  mutate(
    dist_ch_mi = as.numeric(
      st_distance(tract_pts, city_hall)
    ) / 5280
  )

# Review distance distribution
summary(tracts$dist_ch_mi)

4E: Your turn
Build at least three spatial features from your own layers, and use at least two types (count, density, nearest distance, distance to a place). After each one, fit a model, cross-validate it, and log it.


Code
# Baseline model
f1 <- y ~ median_income + pct_renter +
  pct_no_vehicle + pct_bachelors

# Spatial feature 1: Burglary count
f2 <- update(f1, . ~ . + n_burglary)

# Spatial feature 2: Burglary density
f3 <- update(f1, . ~ . + burglary_per_sqmi)

# Spatial feature 3: Distance to nearest street defect
f4 <- update(f1, . ~ . + dist_defect_mi)

# Spatial feature 4: Distance to City Hall
f5 <- update(f1, . ~ . + dist_ch_mi)

# Fit and cross-validate each model
m2 <- lm(f2, data = tracts)
m3 <- lm(f3, data = tracts)
m4 <- lm(f4, data = tracts)
m5 <- lm(f5, data = tracts)

# Record model performance
model_log <- model_log %>%
  add_row(
    model = "m2",
    added = "Burglary count",
    cv_rmse = cv_rmse(f2, tracts),
    notes = "Count feature"
  ) %>%
  add_row(
    model = "m3",
    added = "Burglary density per square mile",
    cv_rmse = cv_rmse(f3, tracts),
    notes = "Density feature"
  ) %>%
  add_row(
    model = "m4",
    added = "Distance to nearest street defect",
    cv_rmse = cv_rmse(f4, tracts),
    notes = "Nearest-distance feature"
  ) %>%
  add_row(
    model = "m5",
    added = "Distance to City Hall",
    cv_rmse = cv_rmse(f5, tracts),
    notes = "Distance-to-place feature"
  )

4 m4    Distance to nearest street defect    5.16 Nearest-distance feature     
5 m5    Distance to City Hall                5.12 Distance-to-place feature    




Interpretation: Which Spatial Features Improved Prediction?
Among the four spatial features tested, distance to Philadelphia City Hall produced the largest improvement in predictive performance. Adding this variable reduced the 10-fold cross-validation RMSE from 5.1513 minutes in the baseline model to 5.1233 minutes. Although the improvement is small, it suggests that geographic proximity to the city center may provide information not fully captured by socioeconomic characteristics.
In contrast, burglary counts, burglary density, and distance to the nearest street defect report slightly increased the CV RMSE. These features may reflect neighborhood conditions, but they do not necessarily capture the transportation accessibility factors that determine commute times. Their limited predictive value may also reflect differences in reporting patterns and the indirect relationship between these indicators and commuting behavior.
Overall, the results suggest that distance to the city center is a more useful spatial predictor than the neighborhood incident indicators tested here. However, the small improvement should be interpreted cautiously.

title: Assignment: Building Features, Watching What Happens
text:
Part 5: Transforming features
Watch the October 9 recorded lecture before you start this part. Below is a summary to work from.
So far, every predictor has entered the model as a straight line: each additional unit of X changes predicted Y by the same amount, everywhere. Transformations let the model bend. For prediction, the question is simply does the bend lower CV RMSE? For interpretation, each transformation changes what a coefficient means, so you need to know how to read it.






TipTransform predictors, not your outcome



Keep your outcome y untransformed in this assignment. If you model log(y), your CV RMSE comes out in log units and can’t be compared to the other rows in your log. (Predicting a logged outcome well requires back-transforming, which is an A4 topic.)



5A: Logs, for skewed predictors
Many urban variables are skewed: a few tracts have huge values, and most have small ones. Income, density, and counts are typical. A log compresses the long tail, so a model can use the difference between 1 and 10 as well as the difference between 100 and 1,000.


Code
library(patchwork)

p1 <- ggplot(tracts, aes(x = burglary_per_sqmi)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30, fill = "#176B4A", color = "#F8F5EE") +
  labs(
    title = "Before Transformation",
    x = "Residential burglaries per square mile",
    y = "Number of census tracts"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

p2 <- ggplot(tracts, aes(x = log1p(burglary_per_sqmi))) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30, fill = "#C3A15D", color = "#F8F5EE") +
  labs(
    title = "After Log Transformation",
    x = "log(1 + burglaries per square mile)",
    y = "Number of census tracts"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

(p1 + p2) +
  plot_annotation(
    title = "Distribution of Burglary Density",
    subtitle = "Philadelphia census tracts | ACS 2019–2023"
  ) &
  theme(
    plot.background = element_rect(fill = "#F8F5EE", color = NA),
    plot.title = element_text(color = "#173F34", face = "bold")
  )











Interpretation: Log Transformation of Burglary Density
The original distribution of residential burglary density is strongly right-skewed, with most census tracts reporting relatively low densities and a small number showing exceptionally high values.
Applying the log1p transformation compresses these extreme values and produces a more balanced distribution while preserving zero-valued observations.
Although the transformation reduces skewness, its usefulness for predicting mean commute time must be evaluated through cross-validation rather than the distribution alone.






Warninglog(0) doesn’t exist



log(0) is -Inf, and it will break your model. Counts and densities often include zeros. Use log1p(x), which computes log(x + 1), for anything that can be 0.


Reading the coefficient: when a predictor is logged, a 1% increase in X goes with a change of about β/100 in Y, in Y’s units. With log1p, this reading is approximate for small values of X.


5B: Squared terms, for curves
If your scatterplot bends (rising and then flattening, or falling and then rising), a squared term lets the line curve. Write it with I(), which tells R to do the arithmetic rather than read ^ as formula syntax.


Code
# Test a nonlinear relationship with distance to City Hall
m_sq <- lm(
  y ~ dist_ch_mi + I(dist_ch_mi^2),
  data = tracts
)

Reading the coefficient: you can’t read either coefficient alone anymore. The effect of X depends on where you are along X. A positive linear term with a negative squared term means Y rises with X and then levels off or turns down. Plot the fitted curve to see it:

Interpretation: Nonlinear Relationship Between Distance and Commute Time
The quadratic model reveals an inverted U-shaped relationship between distance to Philadelphia City Hall and mean commute time. Predicted commute times increase with distance from the city center, reaching a peak at approximately 8.5 miles, before gradually declining.
However, the considerable dispersion of observations around the fitted curve indicates that distance alone cannot fully explain commuting patterns. This nonlinear relationship is worth testing alongside the socioeconomic predictors, using cross-validation to determine whether it improves predictive accuracy.


5C: Categorical variables
Sometimes a number works better as groups, either because the relationship isn’t smooth or because the categories are meaningful. You can make categories from any variable with case_when() or cut(), and then make sure R treats them as a factor.


Code
tracts <- tracts %>%
  mutate(
    ring = case_when(
      dist_ch_mi < 2 ~ "Core",
      dist_ch_mi < 5 ~ "Inner",
      TRUE           ~ "Outer"
    ),
    ring = factor(ring, levels = c("Core", "Inner", "Outer"))
  )

Reading the coefficients: R turns a factor with k categories into k − 1 dummy variables. The category left out is the reference level (here, “Core,” the first level). Each coefficient is the difference from the reference: ringOuter is how much higher or lower predicted Y is in outer tracts compared to core tracts, holding everything else in the model constant. To change the reference, use relevel(ring, ref = "Outer").






NoteCheck your group sizes



If a category has only a handful of tracts, its coefficient is unstable, and in cross-validation some folds may not contain it at all. Aim for at least 20 tracts per category.




5D: Your turn
Try at least one of each: a log, a squared term, and a categorical variable. Choose which variables to transform based on your plots, not at random. Log each model.

m_cat_full <- lm(f_cat, data = tracts)

text:
Part 7: Reflection (about 300 words)

Reflection
The results show that spatial features do not necessarily improve prediction accuracy simply because they add more information. My baseline model, using four socioeconomic predictors, produced a cross-validated RMSE of 5.151 minutes. The most useful addition was distance to Philadelphia City Hall with a quadratic term, which reduced CV RMSE to 5.008 minutes, an improvement of approximately 2.8%. This suggests that commute times vary with distance from the city center in a nonlinear way. In contrast, the logarithmic transformation of residential burglary density performed worst, with a CV RMSE of 5.182 minutes. Burglary patterns may reflect neighborhood conditions, but they do not directly measure transportation accessibility.
In the final model, the coefficient for distance to City Hall is 1.649, while its squared term is −0.09676. The β̂ interpretation is that the marginal association between distance and predicted commute time depends on distance itself: each additional mile changes predicted commute time by approximately (1.649 - 0.19352d) minutes, where (d) is the distance in miles, holding other predictors constant. For the ŷ interpretation, a tract located five miles from City Hall has a distance-related contribution of approximately 5.83 minutes to its predicted commute time, in addition to the intercept and socioeconomic predictors.
Comparing the residual maps, several clusters of overprediction and underprediction remain even after the quadratic transformation. I would next investigate public transit accessibility, particularly access to frequent transit services and travel times to major employment centers. Historical SEPTA route and schedule data could help construct these measures.

check_na <- function(formula, df) {
  vars <- all.vars(formula)
  bad <- vars[sapply(vars, function(v) any(is.na(df[[v]])))]
  if (length(bad) > 0) {
    stop("These variables have NAs: ", paste(bad, collapse = ", "),
         ". Fill them or choose another variable (Rule 1).")
  }
}

# 10-fold CV RMSE, same folds every time
cv_rmse <- function(formula, data) {
  df <- if (inherits(data, "sf")) st_drop_geometry(data) else data
  check_na(formula, df)
  set.seed(5080)
  fit <- train(formula, data = df, method = "lm",
               trControl = trainControl(method = "cv", number = 10))
  fit$results$RMSE
}

# Each house's prediction from the fold where it was held out
cv_pred <- function(formula, data) {
  df <- if (inherits(data, "sf")) st_drop_geometry(data) else data
  check_na(formula, df)
  set.seed(5080)
  fit <- train(formula, data = df, method = "lm",
               trControl = trainControl(method = "cv", number = 10,
                                        savePredictions = "final"))
  fit$pred %>% arrange(rowIndex) %>% pull(pred)
}

# Chicago Data Portal (Socrata) -> sf. `where` is a SoQL filter.
socrata_get <- function(dataset, where, select = NULL, limit = 200000) {
  where <- str_squish(where)
  q <- paste0("$where=", URLencode(where, reserved = TRUE), "&$limit=", limit)
  if (!is.null(select)) q <- paste0(q, "&$select=", URLencode(str_squish(select), reserved = TRUE))

3.1 Market Sale Cleaning
We excluded 1,232 training records flagged as multi-sales (is_multisale = 1), because their recorded prices may represent multiple parcels rather than a single property. This reduced the training dataset from 23,200 to 21,968 sales (5.3% removed).
We retained the remaining sales, including lower-priced transactions, because a low price alone does not establish that a transaction was non-market. No test records were removed.


3.2 Missing Value Treatment
Missing predictor values were imputed using the median for numeric variables and the most frequent value for binary variables. Replacement values were calculated from the cleaned training data only. No additional training records were removed, and all training predictors now have complete values.

5 Part 1: Clean and Explore
Decide which training sales are market sales. Record each rule, why, and how many it removed. Then explore: at least four plots, including a map of price.

5.1 Market Sale Cleaning
We excluded 1,232 training records flagged as multi-sales (is_multisale = 1), because their recorded prices may represent multiple parcels rather than a single property. This reduced the training dataset from 23,200 to 21,968 sales (5.3% removed).
We retained the remaining sales, including lower-priced transactions, because a low price alone does not establish that a transaction was non-market. No test records were removed.


5.2 Missing Value Treatment
Missing predictor values were imputed using the median for numeric variables and the most frequent value for binary variables. Replacement values were calculated from the cleaned training data only. No additional training records were removed, and all training predictors now have complete values.

Our exploratory analysis highlighted four important patterns that informed our modeling approach. First, sale prices were strongly right-skewed, suggesting the need to evaluate prediction errors carefully, particularly for expensive properties. Second, building size showed a positive relationship with sale price, supporting its use as a predictor.
Third, the price map revealed geographic differences, suggesting that spatial features may help explain variation in housing values. Finally, median sale prices differed across 2023–2025, indicating that sale year may also be relevant. Together, these findings motivate a model that considers property characteristics, location, and time rather than relying on a single predictor.

check_na <- function(formula, df) {
  vars <- all.vars(formula)
  bad <- vars[sapply(vars, function(v) any(is.na(df[[v]])))]
  if (length(bad) > 0) {
    stop("These variables have NAs: ", paste(bad, collapse = ", "),
         ". Fill them or choose another variable (Rule 1).")
  }
}

# 10-fold CV RMSE, same folds every time
cv_rmse <- function(formula, data) {
  df <- if (inherits(data, "sf")) st_drop_geometry(data) else data
  check_na(formula, df)
  set.seed(5080)
  fit <- train(formula, data = df, method = "lm",
               trControl = trainControl(method = "cv", number = 10))
  fit$results$RMSE
}

# Each house's prediction from the fold where it was held out
cv_pred <- function(formula, data) {
  df <- if (inherits(data, "sf")) st_drop_geometry(data) else data
  check_na(formula, df)
  set.seed(5080)
  fit <- train(formula, data = df, method = "lm",
               trControl = trainControl(method = "cv", number = 10,
                                        savePredictions = "final"))
  fit$pred %>% arrange(rowIndex) %>% pull(pred)
}

# Chicago Data Portal (Socrata) -> sf. `where` is a SoQL filter.
socrata_get <- function(dataset, where, select = NULL, limit = 200000) {
  where <- str_squish(where)
  q <- paste0("$where=", URLencode(where, reserved = TRUE), "&$limit=", limit)
  if (!is.null(select)) q <- paste0(q, "&$select=", URLencode(str_squish(select), reserved = TRUE))
  url <- paste0("https://data.cityofchicago.org/resource/", dataset, ".geojson?", q)
  tmp <- tempfile(fileext = ".geojson")
  resp <- tryCatch(download.file(url, tmp, quiet = TRUE), error = function(e) e)
  if (inherits(resp, "error")) stop("Portal request failed. Open this URL in a browser to see why:\n", url)
  st_read(tmp, quiet = TRUE)
}

Answer: What in your exploration shaped your modeling choices?
Your answer: Four things shaped our plan. First, prices are strongly right-skewed: the median cleaned sale is $300,000 but the mean is about $430,000, with a long tail into the millions. Rule 4 keeps the outcome in dollars, so RMSE will be driven by the expensive houses, and we expect our biggest misses there. We can’t log the outcome, but we can log skewed predictors. Second, the flexible curves for building size and building age do not follow the straight lines, so we will test log() and squared (I(x^2)) terms and keep them only if CV RMSE improves. Third, the price map shows that prices cluster by place. A structure-only model will leave spatially clustered errors, and Rule 5 bars features built from neighbors’ prices, so we will build location features from open data: tract characteristics from the ACS, distances to amenities, crime exposure (buffer counts and kNN distances), and neighborhood fixed effects. Fourth, the median price rose from $283,000 in 2023 to $310,000 in 2024 and $321,900 in 2025, so sale year and quarter belong in the model as categories.

title: A Nightmare in Regression Class
text:
4 Part 2: Build the model
Start with a structure-only baseline. Then add features in steps you can learn from, logging each one. Keep the log in a tibble with columns model, added, cv_rmse, moran_i, notes.
Every model is scored the same way: 10-fold CV RMSE on the same folds (the provided cv_rmse()), and global Moran’s I of the out-of-fold residuals, using each house’s 5 nearest training sales as neighbors. Residual = actual − predicted, so a positive residual means the model guessed too low. A falling Moran’s I means the errors are clustering less in space.
Rule check for every feature below: nothing is built from a sale price. The Assessor could compute every one of them for a house that did not sell.

4.1 Scoring helpers and the model log


Reveal the Code
# Spatial weights: each training house's 5 nearest training sales
w_knn <- nb2listw(knn2nb(knearneigh(st_coordinates(train), k = 5)), style = "W")

# Global Moran's I of a residual vector
moran_of <- function(resid) as.numeric(moran.mc(resid, w_knn, nsim = 499)$statistic)

# Score one formula: CV RMSE, out-of-fold residuals, Moran's I
score_model <- function(f) {
  resid <- train$sale_price - cv_pred(f, train)
  list(cv_rmse = cv_rmse(f, train),
       moran_i = moran_of(resid),
       resid   = resid)
}

model_log <- tibble(model = character(), added = character(),
                    cv_rmse = numeric(), moran_i = numeric(), notes = character())
resids <- list()   # out-of-fold residuals of every model, for the Part 3 maps




4.2 M1: Structure-only baseline
Every house feature in the file. fireplace_missing is the flag from Part 1.

          cv_rmse = s1$cv_rmse, moran_i = s1$moran_i,

4.8 M7: Neighborhood characteristics from the Census
Houses in tracts with higher incomes, more college graduates and fewer vacant homes should sell for more, even after distance and crime. We take 2019–2023 ACS 5-year estimates for Cook County tracts and give each house the values of the tract it sits in. Income is skewed, so we log it. 4.9 M8: Community area fixed effects
Chicago’s 77 community areas each carry things we did not measure: reputation, schools, lake access, history. A fixed effect lets every area have its own intercept. Boundaries come from the Chicago Data Portal (igwz-8jzy).

Answer: What helped most, and what disappointed you? Use your log.
Based on our model log, adding community area fixed effects (M8) produced the largest improvement. CV RMSE decreased from approximately $222,143 in M7 to $196,562 in M8, while residual Moran’s I decreased from approximately 0.344 to 0.193. This suggests that neighborhood-level differences explain an important part of Chicago housing prices that our earlier variables did not capture.
Adding neighborhood socioeconomic characteristics in M7 also improved prediction substantially. However, the earlier structural and nonlinear features delivered relatively modest improvements, and adding distance-based features did not eliminate spatial clustering. Even our final model retains some spatial autocorrelation, meaning there are still location-specific patterns it cannot fully explain.
Overall, the results show that housing prices depend not only on building characteristics but also on the neighborhoods where properties are located.

6.1 4A. Where does the model fail worst?
Our final model (M8) has the largest mean absolute prediction errors in Lincoln Park ($504,283), Near North Side ($424,419), and Lake View ($322,603). These neighborhoods contain properties with substantial price variation, which may not be fully captured by our predictors.
In Lincoln Park, the model slightly underpredicts sale prices on average, with a mean residual of +$3,451. In Near North Side and Lake View, it slightly overpredicts prices, with mean residuals of -$1,322 and -$1,127, respectively. However, these average errors are relatively small compared with the mean absolute errors, suggesting that large overpredictions and underpredictions often cancel each other out.
This shows that community area fixed effects helped improve our model, but they cannot fully capture differences between individual properties, especially in neighborhoods with expensive and diverse housing markets.


6.2 4B. Does the assessment ratio differ by neighborhood income?
Yes. The median predicted-to-actual sale price ratio increases across neighborhood income groups, from 0.971 in the lowest-income neighborhoods to approximately 1.016 in the highest-income neighborhoods. The middle-income groups have median ratios of 0.987 and 0.995.
This suggests that our model slightly underpredicts home values in lower-income neighborhoods and slightly overpredicts values in higher-income neighborhoods. At the median, this is different from the regressive assessment pattern discussed in The Tax Divide, where lower-income homeowners face a disproportionate tax burden.
However, the mean assessment ratios are above 1 across all income groups, with the largest mean ratio in the lowest-income group (1.31). This indicates that some properties experience substantial overprediction, even when the median suggests underprediction. The difference between the mean and median is important when evaluating potential assessment inequities.
Our Part 1 cleaning rules excluded multi-parcel sales and transactions below $20,000. While these rules helped remove unusual transactions, they may also affect which properties are represented in our analysis, particularly in lower-income neighborhoods.
Finally, these are predictions from our model, not actual property tax assessments. Therefore, we cannot conclude that our model produces the same tax inequities described in The Tax Divide. However, the differences across income groups suggest that fairness should be evaluated carefully before using this type of model for property assessment.

8 Part 6: Reflection (about 300 words, as a team)

8.1 1. Reading a Coefficient Twice
In our final model (M8), the coefficient for building_000sf is approximately 175,638.8. Statistically, this means that a one-unit increase in building size, equivalent to 1,000 square feet, is associated with a $175,638.80 increase in predicted sale price, holding all other variables constant.
From a prediction perspective, if two houses have identical characteristics except that one is 1,000 square feet larger, our model predicts that the larger house will sell for approximately $175,639 more. This illustrates how structural characteristics directly influence the model’s estimated property values.


8.2 2. Would We Recommend This Model to the Assessor?
We would recommend Model 8 as a useful starting point, but not as a fully automated assessment system. Our final cross-validation RMSE was $196,561.80, a substantial improvement over the baseline model. Adding neighborhood fixed effects, census characteristics, crime exposure, and accessibility measures helped capture important differences across Chicago.
However, the model still has limitations. The largest mean absolute errors occurred in Lincoln Park ($504,283), Near North Side ($424,419), and Lake View ($322,603). These neighborhoods may contain expensive or unusual properties that are difficult to predict accurately.
We also found differences in assessment ratios across neighborhood income groups. The median ratio increased from 0.971 in the lowest-income areas to 1.020 in the highest-income areas. Although this pattern differs from the regressive assessment problem described in The Tax Divide, it demonstrates why prediction accuracy and equity should be evaluated together.
Before using the model for taxation, we would recommend additional validation, reviewing unusual properties, checking the timing of external data, and regularly monitoring neighborhood-level errors.
